definition: Anecdotal means based on personal stories rather than systematic evidence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word anecdotal. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know anecdotal should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The professor granted that cold-plunge fans swear by the habit, but she called the benefits anecdotal until someone counts them properly.
Untested is milder than anecdotal — it says no one has checked the claim yet, not that the only support is stories.
Baseless goes further than anecdotal: anecdotal evidence is at least somebody's real experience, while a baseless claim has nothing under it at all.

Story-based support rests on individual accounts rather than measurements — what particular people say happened to them. Anecdotal means the same resting-on-stories, but adds a quiet verdict: in serious writing it concedes the stories are real while denying them the weight of evidence.

Hearsay is what circulates at second hand — you repeat what someone told you someone else saw. Anecdotal accounts are usually firsthand: the teller lived it. Both fall short of systematic evidence, but hearsay adds distance from the event, while anecdotal keeps the witness and loses only the rigor.

Anecdotal means based on personal stories rather than systematic evidence.
At the town meeting, eleven neighbors described smoother commutes since the roundabout opened, and the council nearly voted on the spot.
The traffic engineer held up a hand: the improvement was still anecdotal — eleven happy drivers is a start, not a measurement — and the sensor study would report within the month.
Anecdotal does not mean false; every story may be true.
It means the support is personal experience rather than systematic evidence, and that is the critical force the SAT tests: anecdotal evidence is the charming kind that proves the least.
In test passages and serious writing, anecdotal is quietly damning: it concedes the stories are real while denying them the weight of evidence.
Use hearsay for rumor at second hand; use anecdotal when true-enough personal accounts are offered where data belongs.

When the town replaced its four-way stop with a traffic circle, the letters page filled within a week.
Drivers wrote that the circle had saved them from certain collisions; one cyclist described three near-misses in the month before the change and none after.
At the council meeting, the traffic engineer thanked the writers and then set the letters aside as anecdotal: real experiences, honestly told, but stories all the same.
What the decision needed, she said, was the collision ledger -- every fender bender for five years, counted the same way.
The ledger showed crashes down by a third, and the circle stayed; the letters, she noted, had pointed the right way without ever being able to prove it.
